scrollSteps.value: Growing up in the 1990s felt like a communal experience. Before the internet became the internet we all shared similar schedules and moved like a giant ball of rumbling prepubescent anxiety.

But ever so often a cataclysmic event would happen and some of us felt flung to the outer edges of this homogenous bubble by sapphic yearning. Suddenly our timelines didn’t sync up. Did we want to be her or be with her?
We weren’t sure. We felt isolated, believing there was no one out there who understood.
But unbeknownst to us, we inadvertently created shared touchpoints that, as out and proud adults, we still use to connect with one another.

We waited with baited breath for Xena to kiss Gabrielle. We became regular watchers of the nascent WNBA. And we wore out our rented VHSs of Cruel Intentions. Our connections continued to build, even if we couldn’t see them at the time.
This is the story of one such connection.
Meet Ashleé and Jan. We connected in college through Western Kentucky University’s student newspaper. Neither of us had fully acknowledged our queerness — we were hiding in plain sight.
Jan was closeted in high school because she was still figuring out her sexuality and was terrified of the negative impact that coming out would have on the people she respected.

Ashleé grew up knowing she was different, but was unable to put a name on the flutters she felt when certain women popped up on her TV. And as an adult, the bounds of compulsory heterosexuality sucked out the space for her to imagine life as gay woman.

By the time we reconnected in our 30s, Jan was out and married to a woman. Ashleé was divorced from a man and identified as queer. Yet as our paths to discovering and nurturing our queerness diverged, we could still point to the same pivotal moments in popular culture that served as breadcrumbs to our own self discoveries. This is our journey. Maybe you can see yourself in it too.

timelineInstructions.value: Each side of this timeline represents a personal journey: Jan’s on the left and Ashleé’s on the right.

The rainbow lines represent overarching themes, and the dots are events within those themes. You can use the rainbow dots at the top to be reminded of the full theme definition anywhere along the timeline.

When the rainbow lines push in toward the center, that means that either Jan or Ashleé experienced a cultural touchpoint. On the right is Ashleé’s first touchpoint: Kelly Kapowski on Saved by the Bell. Each touchpoint can be attached to multiple themes, or none at all — that’s why these touchpoints appear on Jan’s side along the black line.
When the lines with the same theme collide in the center, that’s a queernection! Here, both Jan And Ashleé felt a Girl Power connection with Lori "Ice" Fetrick on American Gladiators.

Tap any circle with a plus sign to add it to your own personal queer canon list, and tap any circle with an x to remove it. You can manage your list in the events drawer at the bottom. We’ll use this to show the all your queernections later.
